topic: Pimpl Idiom with Unique Pointer Special Member Functions
explanation:
The Pointer to Implementation (Pimpl) idiom is a powerful technique for decoupling a class's interface from its implementation, but its interaction with smart pointers, specifically unique pointers, requires careful handling of special member functions. The core concept is that a class using a unique pointer to a forward-declared implementation type must declare its destructor in the header file but define it in the implementation file. Scott Meyers explains that this is not merely a stylistic choice but a fundamental requirement for correctness.

Meyers' key insight revolves around type completeness. When the compiler generates the destructor for the main class, it also generates code to destroy all member variables. For a unique pointer member, this involves invoking the pointer's own destructor, which in turn calls `delete` on the raw pointer it holds. The `delete` operator is only valid on a complete type; applying it to a pointer to an incomplete type results in undefined behavior, which standard library implementations typically guard against with a static assertion, causing a compile-time error. By defining the class's destructor in the implementation file, after the full definition of the implementation type is visible, you ensure the compiler has the necessary information to generate the correct destruction code.

The same logic of type completeness extends to the move operations. Declaring a custom destructor prevents the compiler from automatically generating move operations. If you want your Pimpl class to be movable (which is highly desirable), you must declare the move constructor and move assignment operator in the header as well. Crucially, their definitions must also be deferred to the implementation file. Even if you simply default them, the `= default` must appear in the source file. For the move assignment operator, the compiler-generated code needs to destroy the old implementation object before assigning the new one. For the move constructor, compilers often generate exception-handling code that might need to destroy the implementation object, again requiring its full definition.

In practice, this means your header file for a Pimpl class will contain the class definition with a unique pointer to a forward-declared `Impl` struct, along with declarations for the destructor, move constructor, and move assignment operator. The corresponding source file will first provide the full definition of the `Impl` struct and then provide the definitions for those special member functions. This out-of-line definition is the cornerstone of making the Pimpl idiom work correctly with unique pointers, enabling the strong compilation firewall benefits without sacrificing proper resource management.

The primary gotcha is that placing `= default` for the destructor or move operations in the header file will lead to compilation errors that can be cryptic, often mentioning an attempt to delete an incomplete type. While using a shared pointer for the Pimpl would sidestep this specific issue due to its type-erased deleter, Meyers advocates for the unique pointer as the default choice because it correctly models the exclusive ownership semantics inherent to the Pimpl idiom and avoids the overhead of reference counting.
practical_example: In a large-scale software project, a core library component uses the Pimpl idiom to hide its dependency on a third-party XML parsing library. By declaring the destructor and move operations in the header and defining them in the source file, the library's author can update or even replace the XML library (changing the `Impl` struct) without forcing any of the application's client code to recompile. This significantly reduces build times and isolates dependencies.
